title: Comparing and ordering fractions and decimals
blurb: Find the greatest, the least or the right order in any mix of fractions, mixed numbers and decimals, and read the direction the question asks for.
question: Your practice scores are 42/50 in reading, 0.83 in math and 5/6 in grammar. Which is your strongest section, and how do you order the three scores from least to greatest?

teach.body: Formally, two fractions can be compared exactly by a common denominator or by cross-multiplying, and any fraction can be compared with a decimal once it is divided out (numerator ÷ denominator). In plain English: you can't fairly compare 3/8 with 0.41 until both are decimals (0.375 and 0.410). Put everything in one form, line the decimals up, then compare place by place from the left.

head: Symbol or word
Meaning
Example
rows: greater than one, less than the other
teach.caption: The symbol's open side faces the larger number.

items: Pad every decimal to three places: 0.580, 0.625, 0.610, 0.600.
Write back in the original forms: 0.58, 3/5, 0.61, 5/8.
Check two neighbors by cross-multiplying: 3/5 vs 5/8 → 3 × 8 = 24 < 5 × 5 = 25, so 3/5 < 5/8. ✓

teach.caption: More digits does not mean bigger: the first place that differs decides.

items: Same numerator: the LARGER denominator is the SMALLER fraction (smaller pieces). 1/8 < 1/6.

teach.body: Before dividing anything, compare each fraction with 1/2. A fraction is more than 1/2 when its numerator is more than half its denominator: 9/16 > 1/2 because 9 > 8, while 6/13 < 1/2 because 6 < 6.5. One option above 1/2 among three below it is your greatest. Use 1 the same way for mixed numbers and improper fractions, and use the memorized benchmarks (1/8 = 0.125, 3/8 = 0.375, 5/8 = 0.625, 2/3 ≈ 0.667) to skip long division.

teach.text: The HESI A2 builds wrong orderings from: "more digits is bigger" (0.125 > 0.2), "bigger denominator is bigger" (1/8 > 1/6), ranking fractions by their numerators, reading 5/8 as 0.58, dividing the wrong way (7/5 as 0.71), and giving the list in descending order when ascending was asked.

teach.h: Scenario: Kevin ranks his practice scores
teach.body: Kevin Nguyen, a nursing applicant, scored 42/50 in reading, 0.83 in math and 5/6 in grammar. Convert: 42 ÷ 50 = 0.84; 0.83 stays; 5 ÷ 6 = 0.8333... Pad and compare: 0.8300 < 0.8333 < 0.8400. Least to greatest: math (0.83), grammar (5/6), reading (42/50). Reading is strongest. Note how close 5/6 and 0.83 are: rounding 5/6 to 0.83 would have made them look tied.

items: Convert to one form (usually decimals), pad with zeros, compare from the left.
Same numerator: larger denominator means smaller fraction; otherwise cross-multiply.
Use 1/2 and the memorized benchmarks to rule options in or out quickly.
Read the direction: ascending is least to greatest; descending is greatest to least.

summary: You can now compare and order any mix of fractions, mixed numbers and decimals by converting to one form, padding and comparing place by place, or by cross-multiplying and using benchmarks. You avoid the digit-count, denominator, numerator and direction traps the HESI A2 sets.

A.q: Which list orders 0.4, 3/8, 0.38 and 0.41 from least to greatest?

whyNot.0: This treats numbers with more digits as larger (0.4 first, 3/8 = 0.375 last); padded, 0.400 is greater than 0.380 and 0.375.
whyNot.1: This is greatest to least, the descending order.
whyNot.3: This treats 0.38 as larger than 0.4 because 38 > 4; compare tenths first: 3 < 4.

whyNot.2: 0.07 = 0.07 and 0.7 = 0.70; 7 hundredths is less than 70 hundredths.

A.q: Which fraction has the greatest value?

whyNot.2: 9/16 has the largest numerator and denominator but the smallest value, 0.5625.

B.q: Which list orders 0.3, 0.25, 1/3 and 2/7 from greatest to least?

whyNot.0: This is least to greatest, the ascending order.
whyNot.1: This places 0.25 above 2/7, but 2/7 ≈ 0.286 is greater than 0.250.
whyNot.2: This treats 1/3 as less than 0.3, but 1/3 = 0.333..., which is greater than 0.300.

B.q: Four clinics report the share of staff who got a flu shot: A 0.68, B 2/3, C 27/40, D 13/20. Which clinic has the highest rate?

whyNot.2: 27/40 = 0.675, which is less than 0.680; it is the closest near miss.

B.q: Four patients each drank part of a 1-liter bottle: 5/16, 1/3, 3/11 and 2/7 of the bottle. Which amount is the least?

whyNot.0: 5/16 has the largest denominator, but its value (0.3125) is not the least.
whyNot.1: 1/3 has the smallest numerator, but at 0.333 it is the greatest of the four.

C.q: Which list orders 1.45, 7/5, 1.35 and 1 3/8 from least to greatest?

whyNot.0: This converts 7/5 as 5 ÷ 7 ≈ 0.71, dividing the wrong way; 7/5 = 1.4.
whyNot.2: This reads 1 3/8 as 1.3 (the digit 3 after the point); 3/8 = 0.375, so 1 3/8 = 1.375.
whyNot.3: This is greatest to least, the descending order.

whyNot.0: 0.305 has more digits but is less than 0.35 (0.305 < 0.350).
whyNot.2: 0.43 is just above 3/7 ≈ 0.4286, so it is outside the range.

C.q: Practice-test scores: Ana 17/20, Ben 0.8, Cara 0.83, Dev 5/6. Which lists the students from highest to lowest score?

whyNot.1: This is lowest to highest, the reverse of what was asked.
whyNot.2: This puts 0.83 above 5/6, but 5/6 = 0.8333... is slightly more than 0.83.
whyNot.3: This puts 5/6 above 17/20, but 17/20 = 0.85 is greater than 0.833...

reteach.title: Ordering is like comparing prices
reteach.question: If one store says $0.4, another says 38 cents, and a third says 3/8 of a dollar, how do you find the cheapest?

blocks.body: Prices only compare fairly in one unit. $0.4 is 40 cents, 38 cents stays 38, and 3/8 of a dollar is 37.5 cents. Now it is obvious: 37.5 < 38 < 40. Converting to decimals and padding with zeros is the same move: 0.375, 0.380, 0.400. Nobody thinks $0.4 is 4 cents at the register, yet "0.4 is less than 0.38" is one of the most common slips on a fraction-and-decimal list.

items: Convert each value to the same form (cents, or decimals).
Line them up with the same number of places.
Compare from the left, then check whether the list should run up or down.

blocks.text: $0.4 is not 4 cents. Padding it to $0.40 shows it is the most expensive of the three.

explain.body: Pad with zeros so every decimal has the same number of places, then compare from the left. The first place that differs decides.

test.why: Padded: 0.3070, 0.3007, 0.3700, 0.0730. Tenths: 3, 3, 3, 0; hundredths of the 3s: 0, 0, 7. So 0.37 is greatest.

whyNot.0: 0.307 = 0.3070, smaller than 0.3700 in the hundredths place (0 < 7).
whyNot.1: 0.3007 has the most digits but is the second smallest.
whyNot.3: 0.073 has 0 tenths, so it is the smallest.

explain.body: For a/b vs c/d, compare a × d with b × c. The bigger cross-product sits with the bigger fraction. 7/9 vs 4/5: 7 × 5 = 35 and 9 × 4 = 36.

whyNot.1: > would need 7/9 to be larger, but 0.777... is less than 0.8.
whyNot.3: ≥ means greater than or equal; 7/9 is neither.

explain.body: Double the numerator and compare it with the denominator. Bigger than the denominator: more than 1/2. Smaller: less than 1/2. 9/16: 18 > 16, so more than 1/2. 7/15: 14 < 15, so less than 1/2.

test.why: Double each numerator: 12, 14, 18, 16. Only 18 is more than its denominator (16), so 9/16 > 1/2. Check: 9/16 = 0.5625.

explain.body: Convert fractions (top ÷ bottom) to decimals, pad, order them, then read the question again: descending means greatest first.

test.q: Which list orders 0.09, 3/40, 1/12 and 0.1 in descending order?

whyNot.0: This is ascending order (least to greatest).
whyNot.1: This treats 0.09 as greater than 0.1 because 9 > 1; padded, 0.09 = 0.09 and 0.1 = 0.10.
whyNot.3: This puts 1/12 above 0.09, but 1/12 = 0.0833..., which is less than 0.0900.
